image.alt: A person in a yellow sweater sits at a laptop in a sunlit home, surrounded by a camera, desk, and plants. Technology rests within the background of daily life.

slides.text:
Technology need not stay
in the foreground

Calm Technology is not about removing technology. It keeps useful information available while redesigning the relationship so technology does not continually demand our attention.

image.alt: A small gray smart speaker sits on a wooden shelf by a window with several white status lights illuminated, showing how information can remain perceptible without a screen.

slides.text:
The issue is not information volume,
but how attention is handled

In 1995, Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown argued that technology should move naturally between the center and periphery of our attention.

Most of the time it should remain in the background, moving forward only when something changes. The goal is not merely less information, but __deciding when and how much attention to request__.

image.alt: A keyboard, small display, and speaker sit on a desk framed by a pink curtain and mint pegboard, suggesting an environment that communicates through peripheral sight and sound.

slides.text:
The periphery is not
an unimportant place

The periphery is what we sense without explicitly focusing on it—like hearing the engine and feeling a car vibrate while watching the road.

Ordinary signals should not interrupt us. Only a changed signal needs to move to the center. This lets us perceive more of a system's state with less information overload.

image.alt: A close view of the volume, microphone, and mute controls on a round gray smart speaker against a dark background, illustrating a device that calls for attention through sound only when needed.

slides.text:
A good signal explains status,
not just sends an alert

Weiser and Brown described the Dangling String, which moved with network traffic. It swayed slowly when the network was quiet, then moved faster and sounded different as traffic increased.

People could sense the state without constantly reading a number, checking details only when something felt unusual. It was __a signal that distinguished when action was needed__.

image.alt: A round robot vacuum moves across a kitchen floor beside a warmly lit dining table, showing automation operating quietly within an ordinary home.

slides.text:
Calm is closer to agency
than to silence

Technology is not Calm simply because it is silent or invisible. People must be able to notice its state when needed, bring it into focus, understand it, and return it to the background.

Does the person—not the environment—retain the right to decide what deserves attention? That is the more important question for judging a product.

image.alt:
Among the technologies that call for me each day,
which one could come forward
__only when needed?__

__only when needed?__

caption.body: Calm Technology is not a method for removing technology. It redesigns how technology handles human attention: communicating status from the periphery most of the time, then moving to the center only when something changes or action is required. The goal is not silence itself, but the agency to decide what deserves our attention.
caption.cta: Which technology in your day could come forward only when it is truly needed?
